en: ŚGS 1.1.1: Now, therefore, we shall explain the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas).
ŚGS 1.1.2: One who is about to return from his teacher’s house should kindle that fire upon which he places the final fuel-stick.
ŚGS 1.1.3: Or [he may kindle] the nuptial fire.
ŚGS 1.1.4: Some say [the initiation should take place] at the time of inheritance.
ŚGS 1.1.5: Or, when the householder has died, the eldest son himself [should perform it].
ŚGS 1.1.6: On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, on the new moon day, or on another [auspicious day].
ŚGS 1.1.7: Some [say] that [the fire should be fetched] according to one's desire or under a [specific] lunar mansion.
ŚGS 1.1.8: One should fetch the fire from any one of the following: a man who has many cattle, a man of the *viṭ* caste, a family, a frying pan, or one who performs many sacrifices.
ŚGS 1.1.9: Some [say it should be done] in the evening and in the morning.
The teachers maintain that the consecration by means of the evening oblation is based on the authority of the Adhvaryu priest.
One should offer the morning full-oblation with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu, or silently.
The times for kindling the fire and for the offering of this rite are explained by those of the Agnihotra.
ŚGS 1.1.13: And [the rule] beginning with "wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder" (yajñopavītī) applies to everything that is possible, because the ritual manuals (kalpa) are one.
ŚGS 1.1.14: Regarding this, they also say:
ŚGS 1.1.15ab: There are the Pākasaṃsthās, the Havissaṃsthās, and likewise the other Soma-saṃsthās.
ŚGS_1.1.15cd: These twenty-one sacrificial terminuses (yajñasaṃsthā) have been proclaimed.
ŚGS_1.2.0: Now follows the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.
ŚGS_1.2.1: At the conclusion of the ritual, there is the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.
Speech, appearance, age, learning, character, and conduct are the [six] qualities.
Learning, however, outweighs all the others.
One should not disregard learning.
Regarding the divine,
the personal, and the sacrificial— these three are declared to be what is heard within the *mantras* and the *brāhmaṇas*.
[One should honor] one who is active in ritual, learned, advanced in Vedic knowledge, and ascetic.
He who feeds him with rice-porridge (*sṛt*) shall not suffer from hunger again. Whatever deity one wishes to satisfy in all ritual acts,
one should indeed make an offering intended for that deity while focusing the mind upon them in this manner.
Sacrificial food offered in such a manner shall never reach the deity anywhere;
it is said that this [impure offering] is a treasure for humans, but a vessel for the gods.
Now, having fasted for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa).

ŚGS 1.3.2: When the sun shines upon the tops of the great trees in the morning, that is the time for the *homa*, which is most conducive to well-being (*svastyayanatama*) among all ritual procedures (*āvṛt*), except where there is a specific instruction to the contrary.

ŚGS 1.3.3: Being cheerful and pure, in a clean and sheltered place, having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) according to the full ritual rules, he offers portions of the *sthālīpāka* to the deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) according to their respective shares.

ŚGS 1.3.4: And in the case of *sthālīpākas*, the acts of taking up [the vessel], placing it [on the fire], and sprinkling water [over the oblation] are performed with the mantras dedicated to the respective deities.
And the rules for the portions [of the oblation] are as follows:
First, however, one should offer to the deities of the Anvārambhaṇīyā sacrifice prior to the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
The time for the New Moon sacrifice has not passed until the Full Moon, and the time for the Full Moon sacrifice has not passed until the New Moon.
ŚGS 1.3.8: Some consider the morning oblation to be performed at the time of the evening oblation when [the morning] has passed.
ŚGS 1.3.9: However, the time for the Agnihotra is indeed fixed, because an expiation is seen prescribed for one who has deviated from the proper time.
ŚGS 1.3.10: For the two daily oblations, one should prepare an offering of either rice, barley, or husked grains.
ŚGS 1.3.11: In the absence [of these], something else that is not prohibited [may be used]. ŚGS 1.3.12: If it be rice, some [teachers] say that it should be washed.
ŚGS 1.3.13: For other [grains], there is no such preparation.
ŚGS 1.3.14: [The offering] is for Agni in the evening; for Sūrya in the morning. ŚGS 1.3.15: And for Prajāpati after both [offerings]; however, silently. ŚGS 1.3.16:
Some [place] a fuel-stick before each oblation.
ŚGS 1.3.17: The sprinkling around [the fire] is as previously described.
ŚGS 1.4.0: Now follows the rule for the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya).
ŚGS 1.4.1: Having risen in the morning and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should study the svādhyāya day after day.

"O God Savitṛ, impel us today," two [verses]; "Depart, O lord of the mind," this hymn; "Righteousness and Truth," this hymn; the remainder of the hymn beginning with "For you, O Ādityas, have looked down"; thus one [verse]; "The swan dwelling in purity," one [verse]; "Homage to the great ones," one [verse]; "From whatever we fear, O Indra," one [verse]; "Now, of sleep," one [verse]; "He who [offends], O King," one [verse]; "O Agni, may splendor be mine," this hymn; and the five [verses] beginning with "May welfare be measured for us."

ŚGS 1.5.1: There are four types of cooked sacrifices (*pākayajña*): the *huta*, the *ahuta*, the *prahuta*, and the *prāśita*. ŚGS 1.5.2: These five take place outside the hall: at the wedding, the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the cutting of the hair (*keśānta*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*). ŚGS 1.5.3: Having smeared [the ground], scraped it, and sprinkled it with water, one should establish the sacred fire (*agni*).
ŚGS 1.5.4: Some [prescribe] kindling the fire by friction at the wedding.
ŚGS 1.5.5: During the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, on an auspicious day, he should take the hand of a maiden.
ŚGS 1.5.6: She should be one who is endowed with the auspicious marks.
ŚGS 1.5.7: She whose limbs are well-proportioned;
ŚGS 1.5.8: whose hairline is even;
ŚGS 1.5.9: and who has two whorls of hair on her neck that turn to the right.
ŚGS 1.5.10: One should know that she will give birth to six heroes.
ŚGS 1.6.0: Now follows the selection of the bridegroom.
ŚGS 1.6.1: When he is about to take a wife, he addresses the suitors as they depart with the verse: "O you who are free from thorns... (RV X.85.20).
ŚGS 1.6.2: Upon approaching, [the bridegroom] takes flowers, fruits, barley, and a water-pot.
ŚGS 1.6.3: Having thrice proclaimed, "I am here, O venerable one!

ŚGS 1.6.4: When the sun has risen, the members of the household stand facing east, while those bringing [the bride] stand facing west; pronouncing the names of their lineages (gotra) and personal names, they choose the maiden.

When both [the bridegroom and the bride] have agreed, they touch the full vessel (pūrṇapātrī), which is mixed with flowers, unhusked grains, barley, and gold, [reciting]: "Unassailable is this, the unassailability of the gods, their vigor; free from imprecation, the protector against imprecation, may I not be subject to imprecation. May I quickly attain another [world]; may I go to truth; place me in prosperity. Then, [the bridegroom], having risen, places his hand on the head of the girl while reciting: "Upon you, [I bestow] progeny," and "I place progeny upon you; I place cattle upon you; I place splendor and Vedic luster upon you. I place progeny upon you; I place cattle upon you; I place splendor and Vedic luster upon you.
ŚGS 1.7.0: Now follows the oblation once the invitation has been accepted.
ŚGS 1.7.1: Having accepted the invitation, he performs the oblation.
ŚGS 1.7.2: Having smeared a square sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with cow dung.

ŚGS 1.7.3: Between the two eastern intermediate directions, one should face south for rites pertaining to the ancestors (pitrya). ŚGS 1.7.4: One should face north for rites pertaining to the gods (daiva).
ŚGS 1.7.5: Some say one should face east only.
ŚGS 1.7.6: Having drawn a line in the middle running toward the north;
ŚGS 1.7.7: To the south of that, one line directed upward from above, one in the middle, and one to the north;
ŚGS 1.7.8: Having sprinkled water over them.
ŚGS 1.7.9: Having led forward the fire with the mantra, "I lead forward the fire with a gracious mind; may it be the gatherer of riches.
Do not harm our elder, nor our youth; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds," or [ŚGS 1.7.10] silently.

ŚGS 1.7.11: He wipes around the fire three times with his hand moistened with water, moving from left to right; this they call *samūhana*. ŚGS 1.7.12: In the rite for the ancestors (*pitrya*), he does it once, moving from right to left.
ŚGS 1.8.0: Now follows the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*).

ŚGS 1.8.1: Now follows the strewing of the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa). ŚGS 1.8.2: He strews it with kuśa grass blades whose tips point eastward, either threefold or fivefold. ŚGS 1.8.3: First in front, then behind, and then again behind.
ŚGS 1.8.4: He covers the roots with the tips [of the grass].
ŚGS 1.8.5: All the enclosures turn toward the south and are oriented toward the north.
ŚGS 1.8.6: Having established the Brahman priest to the south, [he recites] "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ."

Having adorned [the site] with *sumanas* flowers, he brings forth the *praṇītā* water to the north, reciting: "Who leads you? Then, taking *kuśa* grass with his left hand, he pours it out with his right hand.
ŚGS 1.8.10: Having bent the right knee; ŚGS 1.8.11: [having bent] the left knee in rites for the ancestors;
ŚGS 1.8.12: there is no constant requirement for the strewing of grass around the fire during oblations of clarified butter.
Māṇḍūkeya says that this also applies to the daily oblations (*nityāhuti*).

Having measured two or three young *kuśa* blades—uneven, with unbroken tips, and without internal nodes—by the span of a *prādeśa*, he cuts them with a *kuśa* blade [reciting]: "You are purifiers (*pavitra*).
There are either two or three of them.
Holding [the ladle] with its tip pointing eastward, he sprinkles [water] around [the fire] while reciting "The two [verses] addressed to Viṣṇu" (Vaiṣṇavyau).

Having sprinkled water three times around the fire from left to right using two young *kuśa* blades, he takes up the vessel of clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*) while reciting, "Thou art the milk of the great ones."
ŚGS 1.8.19: Having placed [the vessel] over the fire with the mantra, "For strength (iṣe) thee"; ŚGS 1.8.20: Having removed it toward the north with the mantra, "For vigor (ūrje) thee";

ŚGS 1.8.21: Holding two strainers with their tips pointing north, grasping them on both sides with the thumbs and the ring fingers, and making them inclined with their tips pointing upward, he pours them into the clarified butter (ājya).
"By the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the Vasu Sūrya. Thus [is the formula].
ŚGS 1.8.22: The preparation of the clarified butter (ājya) is required everywhere.
ŚGS 1.8.23: One should not offer an oblation with that which has not been prepared.
ŚGS 1.8.24: And [he pours] water into the *sruva* ladle with the mantra, "Of Savitṛ... (VS 1.31). ŚGS 1.8.25: These [waters] are both the *praṇītā* and the *prokṣaṇī*.
ŚGS 1.9.0: Now follows the *ājya-homa* (oblation of clarified butter).
ŚGS 1.9.1: The vessel is the *sruva* ladle.
ŚGS 1.9.2: One grasps it according to its purpose and characteristics.
ŚGS 1.9.3: Having taken the *kuśa* grass with the left hand, one takes the *sruva* by its base with the right hand [reciting]: "Thou art the hand of Viṣṇu."
ŚGS 1.9.4: He offers oblations of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle.

ŚGS 1.9.5: Starting from the north-western part of the fire, he offers continuously toward the south, reciting: "O Agni, you are the guardian... (*tvam agne pramatiḥ*). ŚGS 1.9.6: Starting from the south-western part of the fire, he offers continuously toward the north, reciting: "He whose these snowy mountains... (*yasyeme himavantaḥ*).
The northern portion of the clarified butter belongs to Agni; the southern belongs to Soma.
The other oblations are offered in the middle.
[He offers with: "Agni is the progenitor; may he give me that woman as a wife, svāhā!"
"May Soma be possessed of progeny; may he make me possessed of progeny through her, svāhā!
May Pūṣan be possessed of kinsmen; may he make me possessed of kinsmen through her father, mother, and brothers, svāhā!
(ŚGS 1.9.10). In the offerings of clarified butter, the two constant portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering are not [performed].
Māṇḍūkeya says that this applies also to the daily oblations (nityāhuti).
This interval between the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the universal expiations, and the Prājāpatya is the place for insertion (āvāpasthāna).

When the sacrificial butter is the offering material, one takes hold of the kuśa blades held in the left hand by their tips with the right hand and by their roots with the left; then one anoints their tips in the sruva-spoon, their middle parts in the butter-pot, and their roots as well.

ŚGS 1.9.14: Now, if [the remnants] are in the cooking pots, the top part is in the *sruk* ladle, the middle part in the *sruva* spoon, and the bottom part in the vessel for clarified butter (*ājya-sthālī*). ŚGS 1.9.15: Having cast them into the fire with the mantra, "Thou art the garment of Agni," ŚGS 1.9.16: he should place three fuel sticks upon the fire.
ŚGS 1.9.17: The sprinkling around [the fire] is as previously described.

ŚGS 1.9.18: In cases where no mantra has been prescribed and the deity is not specified, one should offer oblations with the pure utterance of *svāhā*, saying: "To such-and-such [deity], svāhā! To such-and-such [deity], svāhā! ŚGS 1.9.19:
The ritual procedure for the oblation when an invitation has been accepted has been explained.
ŚGS 1.10.0: Now, the varieties of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña).
ŚGS 1.10.1: The archetype (prakṛti) is the Bhūtikaraṇa.
ŚGS 1.10.2: And it applies to all oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti).
ŚGS 1.10.3: [The rules apply] to sacrifices involving animal victims from branches of the Veda; ŚGS 1.10.4: and to the *caru* offerings and the *pākayajñas*.

ŚGS 1.10.5: All these *pākayajñas* are performed without *prayāja* offerings, without *anuyāja* offerings, without the *iḍā* invocation, without the *nigada* formula, and without the *sāmidhenī* verses.

(Regarding the five *prayājas* and the three *anuyājas*, see Hillebrandt, *Neu- und Vollmondopfer*, pp. 94ff and 134ff; regarding the *iḍā*, see p. 122ff; regarding the *nigadas*, see Weber, *ISt.*, i, p. 217, etc.)

Regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses (Hillebrandt, op. cit., pp. 74ff.): ŚGS 1.10.6: "There are also verses on this: ŚGS 1.10.7ab: 'The *agnihotra* is offered by means of the *homa* sacrifice; it is unoffered [in the fire], but offered in the Brahmin.'"
The *prahuta* is that which is offered in the rite for the ancestors; the *prāśita* is that which is consumed by a Brāhmaṇa; and the *huta* is that which is poured into the fire.
One should always offer the oblation (*havis*) while keeping the knees straight and the legs apart.
For the gods never accept an offering made outside [the sacred fire].

Having recited a mantra belonging to Rudra, a Rākṣasa, the ancestors, or Asuras, or one used for malevolent purposes (abhicārika), he should touch water and touch himself. Now follows the ritual for Indrāṇī.
ŚGS 1.11.1: Now, on this night, or tomorrow, or the third day, they will say, "The girl is to be given.
ŚGS 1.11.2: When that night has passed and the time of dawn has arrived, having bathed the girl—including her head—with the finest fruits of all medicinal herbs mixed with fragrant substances;
ŚGS 1.11.3: and having caused her to put on a red garment or an unwashed one.

ŚGS 1.11.4: Having seated the girl to the west of the fire, while she maintains contact [with him], he offers oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and then offers oblations of clarified butter: to Agni, to Soma, to Prajāpati, to Mitra, to Varuṇa, to Indra, to Indrāṇī, to Gandharva, to Bhaga, to Pūṣan, to Tvaṣṭṛ, to Bṛhaspati, and to King Pratyānīka. ŚGS 1.11.5:
Four or eight women who are not widows, having gratified them with vegetable cakes, liquor, and food, should perform four circumambulations.
ŚGS 1.11.6: These same deities [are invoked] for a male [child].
ŚGS 1.11.7: [The offerings] to Vaiśravaṇa and Īśāna.
ŚGS 1.11.8: Following this, the feeding of Brahmins. ŚGS 1.12.0: Now, the rite of marriage.

ŚGS 1.12.1: When the bridegroom has bathed and performed the auspicious rites, young women who are fortunate and whose husbands are living lead the maiden to his house. ŚGS 1.12.2: He should not act contrary to their wishes, except in matters concerning forbidden food or sinful acts. ŚGS 1.12.3: Having been permitted by them, he then gives her a garment with the verse, "Raibhī was [the meter]."
ŚGS 1.12.4: With the words, "Thought is the pillow," he takes up the ointment box.
ŚGS 1.12.5: With the words, "May all the gods anoint [her]," she is to be anointed.
ŚGS 1.12.6: "Just as this Śacī, the beloved wife, who has good sons, and just as Aditi..."

With the words, “And may Apālā, who is not a widow, thus protect you here,” he places a *śalalī* porcupine quill with three white stripes into her right hand. With the words, “Form after form,” he places a mirror into her left hand.
Her kinsmen tie a protective amulet (*pratisara*) made of red and black wool or linen, adorned with three gems, upon her, with the words, “Blue and red.”

ŚGS 1.12.9: With the words, "Sweet are the plants," he ties on madhūka flowers. ŚGS 1.12.10: At the wedding, having honored the cow, those two cows for the *madhuparka* [offering] are in the house. ŚGS 1.12.11: Having seated the girl to the west of the fire, while she maintains contact with him, he offers three oblations with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*).
ŚGS 1.12.12: In this injunction, one should understand that the fourth [offering] is to be made with all [the verses] together.
ŚGS 1.12.13: Thus, when there is no specific instruction, in all rites for prosperity, one should offer with these very [verses] both before and after [the main rite].
ŚGS 1.13.0: Now follows the taking of the hand (marriage).

ŚGS 1.13.1: "Become a sovereign queen over your father-in-law," [saying this] the father or brother, standing and facing west while she sits facing east, offers an oblation upon the front of her head with either the *sruk* or the *sruva* ladle. ŚGS 1.13.2: "I take your hand for the sake of good fortune," [saying this] he takes her right hand with his own right hand—grasping it including the thumb—with his palm upward, while she sits facing east and he stands facing west. ŚGS 1.13.3: And having recited the five subsequent verses.

"‘I am he (Ama), you are she (Sā); you are she, I am he. I am heaven, you are earth; you are the Ṛg, I am the Sāman. As such, be devoted to me. Having thus [spoken], and having filled a new water-pot with ‘Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ,’ and having cast into it twigs from a male-named tree that contain sap and leaves, along with Kuśa grass,"
Some say it is gold.
Having given that to a student (brahmacārin) who is restrained in speech,
those [stones] remain in the north-eastern direction, arranged from left to right.
Having placed a stone to the north,
he makes her rise with the words, "Come,
O auspicious lady," and says, "Come, step upon this stone; like a stone, may you be firm."
"Trample those who attack; overcome those who challenge!"— having made [the boy] step upon a stone with the forepart of his right foot,
and having led him around the fire keeping it to his right,
he gives him a second garment with that same mantra.
ŚGS 1.13.15: The father or the brother pours fried grains mixed with *śamī* leaves and *palāśa* leaves into his joined palms.
ŚGS 1.13.16: There is the spreading under [of clarified butter], the sprinkling over, and the subsequent sprinkling over with clarified butter (*ājya*).
ŚGS 1.13.17: He offers them as oblations.

Now follows the taking of seven steps. Standing, she offers an oblation with the mantra: "This noble lady, scattering the parched grains, prays: 'May you be auspicious to our kinsmen; may my husband live long. Svāhā! The husband recites this mantra.
ŚGS 1.14.2: The second [step] is performed in the same manner as the stepping upon the stone and so forth.
ŚGS 1.14.3: The third is performed in the same manner.
ŚGS 1.14.4: The fourth is performed silently by one who desires [to do so].
ŚGS 1.14.5: He causes [the bride] to take seven steps toward the north-eastern direction.

ŚGS 1.14.6: "For sap, one-step; for strength, two-steps; for the increase of wealth, three-steps; for well-being, four-steps; for cattle, five-steps; for the seasons, six-steps; be a friend with seven-steps! ŚGS 1.14.7:
He pacifies those [steps] with water.
Having purified himself with the three *stheyā* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," he should sprinkle water upon his head.
(The verse is: *āpo hi ṣṭhā*).
ŚGS 1.14.9: Having sprinkled [water] on the crown of the head.
ŚGS 1.14.10: He says, "I shall give a cow.
ŚGS 1.14.11: In all ritual acts, such as the *sthālīpāka* and others, he should give something to the Brahmins.
ŚGS 1.14.12: To one who knows the *Sūryā* hymn, he gives the bride's garment (*vādhūya*).
A cow is the preferred gift for a Brāhmaṇa;
a village for a Rājanya;
a horse for a Vaiśya.
He gives a hundred cows with a stallion for the daughter's husband;
he gives a horse to those who perform sacrifices.
Now follows the departure for the house of the bridegroom.

ŚGS 1.15.1: When she is departing from the house, [the husband recites] the triplet beginning with "I release you" (*pra tvā muñcāmi*). ŚGS 1.15.2: When she weeps, [he recites] "Weeping for the living" (*jīvaṃ rudantī*).
ŚGS 1.15.3: Then the wife performs the smearing of the axle of the chariot with ghee, using this [verse]: "They have eaten, they have rejoiced" (*akṣann amīmadanta*).
With these two verses, "Pure are your two wheels" and "Your two wheels," he should fasten the two wheels—the first with the first verse and the second with the second.
And [he should fasten] the two oxen.
With the verse "In the hole of the chariot's yoke," having driven a single peg into each of the holes for the pins of a fruit-bearing tree, he should fix them.
ŚGS 1.15.7: Or, having consecrated them with mantras daily;
ŚGS 1.15.8: then they yoke the two oxen with the two verses beginning, "May thy right [ox] be yoked," and with the half-verse, "The two bright oxen. Having consecrated the yoked pair, ŚGS 1.15.9:
then, if a part of the chariot should break or be cut, after having led a maiden into the house of the one who has established the sacred fires;
ŚGS 1.15.10: With the verse, "Clothe yourself in the wood of the *khadira*," he should fasten [the garment].
ŚGS 1.15.11: With the verse, "That very horse," he should tie a knot. ŚGS 1.15.12: He mutters the five-verse hymn beginning with, "May they measure out well-being for us."
While she is mounting the chariot, [he recites]: "The *kiṃśuka* tree.
At the crossroads, [he recites]: "May no waylayers find us.
At the cemetery, [he recites]: "Those who [harm] the bride."
ŚGS 1.15.16: He mutters the half-verse, "O tree, with a hundred branches," over a tree.
ŚGS 1.15.17: He recites, "The good protectress," while she is boarding a boat. ŚGS 1.15.18: He recites, "The stony one," while she is crossing a river.
Or rather, [she may enter] while it is still yoked.
With the verse "Upward your wave," she enters a place that is not deep.
With the verse "Here is what is dear," he causes her to pass by seven houses once she has reached them.
ŚGS 1.16.0: Now follows the leading of [the bride] to the house.
ŚGS 1.16.1: It has been stated [in the preceding section]: "He brings her. ŚGS 1.16.2: Having seated her there, while she maintains contact with him, the husband offers four oblations.

"By the god Agni, by the world of the earth, among the worlds; by the Ṛgveda, among the Vedas—with that I pacify you, O [Name], svāhā! By the god Vāyu, by the world of the atmosphere, among the worlds; by the Yajurveda, among the Vedas—with that I pacify you, O [Name], svāhā! By the god Sūrya, by the world of heaven, among the worlds; by the Sāmaveda, among the Vedas—with that I pacify you, O [Name], svāhā!"

"By the god Candra, by the world of the quarters, by the worlds, by the Brahman, by the Veda—by that I pacify you, O [Name], svāhā! Bhūḥ! That mark of yours which brings ruin to the husband, which slays the brother-in-law, which slays the paramour—that I make [non-existent] for you, O [Name], svāhā! Or, with the first *mahāvyāhṛti*, the first [mark] is touched; with the second, the second; with the third, the third; and with all [three] together, the fourth.
With the mantra "Not of terrible aspect," he should wipe the two eyes with an application of clarified butter.

ŚGS 1.19.1: Having ground the root of adhyāṇḍā, one should pour it into the right nostril at the time of her season with the two verses beginning "Arise, O woman, you have a husband," ending with the utterance of *svāhā*.

In the male, indeed, there is semen; he pours that into the female.

Prajāpati ordained it; Savitṛ fashioned it.
May he, avoiding the jealousy toward women, place a male child here;
may he bestow a son upon us. Whatever auspicious seeds men beget for us, through those you shall give birth to a son; be a prolific mother, like a milch-cow.
Cry out, take courage, place the embryo, and bring it to completion!
O bull, place the seed; we invoke you for the sake of progeny. May a male son be conceived within the womb of her whose seed you, O Lord, have taken up.
"Fill him up; let him who has been ten months in the womb be born as the most excellent among his own kin"—or [one may say this].

Under the asterism Puṣya or Śravaṇa,

ŚGS 2.7.7: Having first grasped them with his left hand, the teacher, sprinkling them with water with his right hand, then causes the other to recite.

ŚGS 2.7.10: “Recite the Gāyatrī to me, sir,” says the other; “I shall recite the Gāyatrī to you,” says the teacher. ŚGS 2.7.11: “Recite the Vaiśvāmitrī to me, sir,” says the other; “I shall recite the Vaiśvāmitrī (or Vaiśvānarī) to you,” says the teacher.

ŚGS 2.7.12: “O Sage, recite [the Ṛṣis] for me,” says the other. “I shall recite the deities for you,” says the teacher. ŚGS 2.7.13: “O Sage, recite the deities for me,” says the other. “I shall recite the deities for you,” says the teacher. ŚGS 2.7.14: “O Sage, recite the meters for me,” says the other. “I shall recite the meters for you,” says the teacher.

ŚGS 2.7.15: "Recite the *śruti*, sir! says the other; "I recite the *śruti* to you," says the teacher. ŚGS 2.7.16: "Recite the *smṛti*, sir! says the other; "I recite the *smṛti* to you," says the teacher. ŚGS 2.7.17: "Recite faith and intelligence (*śraddhā-medhe*), sir! says the other; "I recite faith and intelligence to you," says the teacher.

ŚGS 2.7.18: In this manner, whatever mantra belongs to whichever seer (ṛṣi), whichever deity, and whichever metre, he should recite that very mantra accordingly. ŚGS 2.7.19: Or, if he cannot find the seer, deity, and metre, [he should recite] this [verse]: "tatsaviturvareṇyam. He should recite it foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally without pausing—"this is it," says the teacher at the conclusion. ŚGS 2.7.20: In this way, he should recite each individual seer or each section (anuvāka).

ŚGS 2.7.21: [He should recite] one section from the *kṣudrasūkta* hymns; 2.7.22: or as much as the teacher may deem appropriate; 2.7.23: or he may, at will, recite the first and last verses of a hymn belonging to a seer (*ṛṣi*).
ŚGS 2.7.24: Or [he may recite] an entire section (anuvāka). ŚGS 2.7.25: Or he may recite one verse at the beginning of each hymn (sūkta). ŚGS 2.7.26:
The teacher may, at his discretion, say "beginning with this" at the start of a hymn.
This has been explained in the *Ṛṣisvādhyāya*.
When it is completed, having taken young *kuśa* grass and having made a pit at the root with the hide of a bull, he pours water onto the *kuśa* grass according to the hymn (*sūkta*).
For the remainder of the day, there is staying in place and fasting.

ŚGS 2.8.1: In the afternoon, having begged for uncrushed grains (*akṣatadhānā*), he should offer them into the fire with his hand according to the rules for *ājya* oblations, reciting the remainder of the hymn verse by verse, beginning with "The wonderful guardian of the assembly" (*sadasas patim adbhutam*). ŚGS 2.8.2: Having caused the teacher to pronounce a blessing (*svasti*) with sacrificial foods (*bhakṣa*), ŚGS 2.9.0:
Now follows the ritual of the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).

ŚGS 2.9.1: In the forest, with fuel-sticks in hand, he constantly performs the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), restrained in speech, facing north-east, in a place to the west of the eighth [part of the sky], until the appearance of the stars.
ŚGS 2.9.2: When [the time] has passed, having muttered the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), the Sāvitrī, and the benedictory hymns (*svastyayana*).
ŚGS 2.9.3: Likewise in the morning, standing and facing east, until the appearance of the solar disc.
ŚGS 2.10.0: Now, the fire-ritual (agnikārya). ŚGS 2.10.1: Once the sun has risen, the study [of the Veda] begins.
ŚGS 2.10.2: This occurs day by day, both evening and morning.
ŚGS 2.10.3: Having kindled the fire, swept around it, and sprinkled water around it, and having bent his right knee;
ŚGS 2.10.4: "I have brought a fuel-stick for Agni, the great Jātavedas.
May Jātavedas grant me faith and wisdom, svāhā!"
You are fuel; may we prosper. You are kindling; you are splendor; bestow splendor upon me. Svāhā!
Being kindled, prosper me with progeny and with wealth. Svāhā!
"O Agni, this is your fuel-stick; grow by it and swell;
may we also grow and swell, svāhā!
Having thus sprinkled water around the fire, he proceeds.
ŚGS 2.10.6: "May this Agni Jātavedas, being praised, grant me faith, intelligence, non-falling [from grace], and mindfulness; may he bestow prosperity upon us. With these words, he worships the fire.

ŚGS 2.10.7: (He applies the *tripuṇḍra* mark with ashes on five places—the forehead, the heart, the right shoulder, the left, and then the back—using five mantras, one for each, according to the *Tryāyuṣa* rite spoken by Suparṇa, as seen in the practice of the elders.)
ŚGS 2.10.8: He who, having thus offered oblations, stands before the fire, studies one, two, three, or all of these Vedas.
ŚGS 2.11.0: Now follows the ritual procedure for the Śukriya vow.
ŚGS 2.11.1: Now follows the instruction regarding the vow.
The ritual procedure for him is explained by [the rules for] the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
He does not recite the *Sāvitrī*.
According to some, [the procedure ends] with the handing over of the staff (*daṇḍa-pradāna*).
ŚGS 2.11.5: During the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight;

ŚGS 2.11.6: Having entered upon the student life (brahmacarya), the teacher—abstaining from meat (and remaining a celibate student)— ŚGS 2.11.7: [should do so] avoiding the fourteenth and the eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
Some [teachers] say that it applies to the first and the last [nights].
Or, he should prescribe the *brahmacarya* vow for her who is the *śukriya* (the wife) or whom he considers to be otherwise unpraiseworthy.
He should observe the *brahmacarya* vow for three nights, twelve nights, a year, or for as long as the teacher deems necessary.
The Śākvara [chant] lasts for one year;
the Vrātika and Aupaniṣada [chants] likewise.

When the time is complete and the period of studentship has been performed, and when the Veda has been recited up to the end of the Śamyor Bārhaspatya, one who intends to have the secret (rahasya) portion heard should observe the rules regarding the time according to the instruction.

ŚGS 2.12.0: Now follows the rite of looking up (udīkṣaṇikā). ŚGS 2.12.1: Having finished his morning meal, in the afternoon, in the direction that is not defeated (the north-east), ŚGS 2.12.2: having offered the oblation, the teacher then asks him concerning those very deities to whom he has been dedicated: "In Agni, Indra, Āditya, and the Viśvedevas, you have practiced the life of a religious student (brahmacarya)."
When [the student] has replied, "I have eaten,
sir," the teacher, standing behind the fire and in front of the student who is facing east, wraps the unwashed garment three times around the student's face from left to right;
having placed the fringe at the top so that it does not slip down.

ŚGS 2.12.6: "Without performing the kindling of the sacred firewood for three nights, without wandering for alms, without sleeping on the ground, and without serving the teacher—remaining restrained in speech and vigilant—dwell in the forest, in a temple, or by the *agnihotra* fire.
ŚGS 2.12.7: Regarding this, some teachers prescribe those very same observances for him while he remains [there] during the night.

ŚGS 2.12.8: The teacher shall abstain from meat and remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). ŚGS 2.12.9: When the three-night period has passed, or when departing from a village at dawn, he shall not look upon these occasions of non-study (*anadhyāya*):

ŚGS 2.12.10: Raw meat, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, a woman in labor, those with flayed hands, a cremation ground, and all corpse-like forms—whatever does not enter his mouth, he must cast out from his dwelling.

ŚGS 2.12.11: Having gone out in a north-easterly direction, the teacher sits down facing east in a clean place. ŚGS 2.12.12: When the sun has risen, he recites [the verses] according to the rule for oral instruction to one who is restrained in speech and wears a turban. ŚGS 2.12.13:
This same rule applies specifically to the Mahānāmnī verses.
ŚGS 2.12.14: Now, while the teacher is engaged in the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) in the subsequent sections, the other [the student] listens.
ŚGS 2.12.15: He gives a turban, a vessel, and a cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
ŚGS 2.12.16: He recites "tvam tam" and "ucca divi," or the whole [text] with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).
ŚGS 2.12.17: Regarding this, some indeed prepare a *vaiśvadeva* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) in all the ritual sections.
ŚGS 2.12.18: According to Māṇḍūkeya, it should be prepared according to one's means.
ŚGS 2.13.0: Now follow the rules concerning the staff (*daṇḍa*).
ŚGS 2.13.1: Now, therefore, follow the rules regarding the staff.
ŚGS 2.13.2: One should not walk between oneself and one's staff.

ŚGS 2.13.3: If, however, any one of the staff, the girdle, or the sacrificial cord should become frayed or broken, the expiation for that is the same as that prescribed for the chariot at the wedding ceremony.
ŚGS 2.13.4: If the girdle cannot be repaired, he makes another one and consecrates it with the following mantra:
ŚGS 2.13.5: "O Goddess Sarasvatī, protector, you who know the distinction between the pure and the impure;
O Girdle, maintain my vow unbroken and uninjured. O Agni, bearer of vows, pure Agni, bring the gods here."
"Come to our sacrifice and our oblation, O guardian of vows, bearing our vows, inviolable; be our messenger, ageless and a hero of noble lineage.
Bestowing jewels and being most gracious, O Agni Jātavedas, protect us that we may live. (ŚGS 2.13.6) Having recited this, he ties the sacrificial cord (*upavīta*) to his staff.
And this too:
when the vow is completed, one should offer into the water the sacrificial cord, the staff, the girdle, and likewise the deerskin,
either with a verse addressed to Varuṇa or with the essence [of the sacrifice].
ŚGS 2.14.0: Now follows the Vaiśvadeva rite.
ŚGS 2.14.1: Now, regarding the Vaiśvadeva:
ŚGS 2.14.2: The ritual procedure for the oblation has been explained.
ŚGS 2.14.3: One should offer the prepared Vaiśvadeva oblation in the domestic fire every morning and evening.

ŚGS 2.14.4: Having offered with the words, "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Indra and Agni! Svāhā to Viṣṇu! Svāhā to Bharadvāja-Dhanvantari! Svāhā to the Viśvedevas! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Aditi! Svāhā to Anumati! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!"—[one offers] to these deities.

ŚGS 2.14.5: Then, one should offer an oblation in the middle of the site to these deities: "Homage to Brahmā and to the Brāhmaṇas! O Vāstoṣpati, acknowledge us! Thus, in the middle of the site, [he offers] to Vāstoṣpati. ŚGS 2.14.6:
Then, he offers an oblation to the quarters, proceeding clockwise according to their respective forms.

ŚGS 2.14.7: "Homage to Indra and to those belonging to Indra; homage to Yama and to those belonging to Yama; homage to Varuṇa and to those belonging to Varuṇa; homage to Soma and to those belonging to Soma; homage to Bṛhaspati and to those belonging to Bṛhaspati."

ŚGS 2.14.8: Then, upon the solar disc: "Homage to Aditi and to the Ādityas; homage to the lunar mansions, to the seasons, to the months, to the half-months, to the days and nights, and to the years. ŚGS 2.14.9: "To Pūṣan, the maker of paths; to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ; and to the Maruts"—thus [one should offer] at the thresholds.
ŚGS 2.14.10: "To Viṣṇu" [is offered] on the grinding stone.
"To the lords of the forest," [he offers] into the mortar; "To the plants," at the place of the plants;
"To Parjanya and the waters," into the water-jar.
ŚGS 2.14.14: "Homage to Śrī on the bed; to Bhadrakālī at the head and at the feet. ŚGS 2.14.15: "In a protected place: Homage to the source of all food. ŚGS 2.14.16:

Then [he offers oblations] in the intermediate space with the mantras "To those who roam by night" in the evening, "To those who roam by day" in the morning, and also with "Those gods... (ye devāsaḥ).
ŚGS 2.14.17: To the unknown deities he offers to the north, and to Dhana-pati as well.
ŚGS 2.14.18: Wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he pours out the remainder to the south with the mantra, "Those who have been consumed by fire...
ŚGS 2.14.19: Having made offerings to the gods, the ancestors, and men, he should feed a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*).
ŚGS 2.14.20: Or he should give alms to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin).

ŚGS 2.14.21: Immediately thereafter, he should feed a woman living in her father’s house, pregnant women, children, and the elderly. ŚGS 2.14.22: He should scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcasts (śvapacas), and birds.
ŚGS 2.14.23: Thus, one should not eat what has not been offered.
ŚGS 2.14.24: Not alone.
ŚGS 2.14.25: Not before [others].
Regarding this, it is also stated in a *ṛc*: "The thoughtless man obtains food in vain.
Now follows the ritual for the sixfold guest-offering (*ṣaḍarghaṇa*).
If any one of the six types of guests worthy of honor should arrive, he should provide a cow, a goat, or food—whichever he considers most appropriate.

ŚGS_2.15.2: The offering should not be without meat. ŚGS_2.15.3: One should say, "Perform [this] for the sacrifice, perform [this] for the wedding. ŚGS_2.15.4: For the teacher, there is an animal dedicated to Agni.
To the officiating priest belongs the offering to Bṛhaspati; to the one who performs the marriage ceremony belongs the offering to Prajāpati;
to the king belongs the offering to Indra.
For a friend, the offering is dedicated to Mitra;
for a *snātaka*, it is dedicated to Indra and Agni.

Even if one should sacrifice with Soma more than once a year, they should perform the sacrifice for him only after the guest-offering (*arghya*) has been prepared, not before the guest-offering has been prepared.
Regarding that, it is also said:
Now follows the ritual for the animal sacrifice (paśukarma):
"At the honey-mixture (madhuparka), at the Soma sacrifice, and at rites for the ancestors or deities."
"Manu has declared that animals are to be sacrificed only here and not elsewhere.
Both the teacher and the father, as well as a friend who is not a guest in the house—whatever these may prescribe, that one should do; such is the dharma ordained."

ŚGS 2.16.3: One should recognize as a guest even a resident of the same village who has returned from a journey, or one who has arrived at the house where the wife and the sacred fires are present. ŚGS 2.16.4:
The fire-sacrifice (*agni-hotra*), the offerings to the spirits (*bali-vardāḥ*), and a guest arriving at the proper time [are all essential].
Both children and family elders burn [the household] when they are treated with disrespect. The draft-ox, the *agnihotra* fire, and the religious student (*brahmacārī*):
these three succeed only while eating; there is no success for them if they do not eat.
ŚGS_2.16.6: The deities approach the householder day by day to seize the person for their share; he ought to offer [the oblation] to them. ŚGS_2.17.0:
Now follows the ritual for guests (atithi-karma).
ŚGS 2.17.1: Even for one who constantly gathers blades of grass and performs the Agnihotra sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa who dwells unhonored takes away all his merit. ŚGS 2.17.2:
The Brahma-yajña is prescribed as being performed until the water-vessel is offered, or even until the wood is offered, or until a hymn (sūkta) or a section (anuvāka) is completed.
There shall be no fasting while away from home; the wife maintains the vow.
His son, brother, wife, or pupil may offer the bali-oblation on his behalf.
Those who perform this Vaiśvadeva rite both morning and evening—
"May they prosper in wealth, long life, fame, and offspring.
Now follows the ritual for a student who is about to depart on a journey.
A student who is about to depart addresses his teacher.
ŚGS 2.18.2: [The student says] "Of the out-breath and in-breath," in a whisper; "Om, I shall dwell, sir! aloud. ŚGS 2.18.3:

[The teacher says] "O out-breath and in-breath, wide-extending one, I enter into you. I entrust him to the god who is the protector. O God Savitṛ, this is your brahmacārī; I entrust him to you. Protect him; do not abandon him," in a whisper. ŚGS 2.18.4: "Om, may it be well! aloud; "May it be well! aloud, [says] the teacher.

ŚGS 3.1.0: Now follows the ritual of returning home (samāvartana). ŚGS 3.1.1: The bath belongs to one who is about to return home. ŚGS 3.1.2: Having seated him upon what is called "the ox-yielding" (anaḍvāh), he causes his hair and beard to be shaved, as well as his body hair and nails.
Having scattered rice, barley, sesame, mustard seeds, and apāmārga plants along with flowers, he sprinkles [the child] with water while reciting the hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭha" (Āpohiṣṭhīya).
(The verse: "āpo hi ṣṭha...")
Having adorned himself and put on two garments with the words,
"You two [put on] the garments," he then fastens a gold necklace upon him with the verse, "Bestowing long life and splendor."

ŚGS 3.1.8: With the mantra "O Agni, [grant] me splendor," he puts on the turban. ŚGS 3.1.9: With the mantra "O invincible one, house by house," he takes up the parasol. ŚGS 3.1.10: With the mantra "Ascend," he puts on the sandals.
ŚGS 3.1.11: With the words, "May your goad be long," he takes up a staff made of bamboo.
ŚGS 3.1.12: On that day, he should remain secluded.
ŚGS 3.1.13: With the verses, "O tree, with strong limbs... and "The ruler thus...", he should mount the chariot.
ŚGS 3.1.14: Wherever they should honor him with a cow or an animal, he should first approach that place.
ŚGS 3.1.15: Or he may return from among cows, or from a fruit-bearing tree.
ŚGS 3.1.16: With the words, "O Indra, bestow upon us the most excellent riches," and "O Earth, be pleasant," he descends.
ŚGS 3.1.17: On that day, he should eat food that is desired.
ŚGS 3.1.18: He should give a pair of garments to the teacher, as well as a turban, a jeweled earring, a staff, sandals, and an umbrella.
ŚGS 3.2.0: Now follows the domestic ritual.

ŚGS 3.2.1: One who intends to have a house built [recites], "I encompass the people here for the sake of food," and having traced a circle three times with a branch of the *udumbara* tree, he offers an oblation upon a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the center. ŚGS 3.2.2: "Who art thou? Whose art thou? For whom doth thou offer? Desirous of a village, I offer, svāhā! In this [place] thou art the portion of the gods; from here the fathers have departed, having been born. Virāj offered the sacrifice desiring a village;
nothing whatsoever was left out of the gods, svāhā! Thus he says.
ŚGS_3.2.3: Having caused pits to be dug for the posts; ŚGS_3.2.4: having poured in water-mixtures;
ŚGS_3.2.5: "I fix this branch of immortality, a stream of honey, furthering the acquisition of riches."

"May this child cry toward her; may the boy cry toward her; may the cow, whose calf is ever-present, cry toward her!"—with these words, he places a branch of *udumbara* smeared with clarified butter into the pit at the southern door-post.
"I raise up this branch of the world, a stream of honey, a furtherer of riches.
May this child cry toward her; may the boy cry toward her; may the cow, whose calf is young, cry toward her!"—with these words, he places it on the north side.
ŚGS_3.2.7: In this manner, [he places them] two by two to the south, behind, and to the north.
ŚGS_3.2.9: "This branch of this tree, dripping with ghee, I place in immortality;
here the infant cries out, the boy; may the cows, ever accompanied by their calves, flow forth"—with these words he raises the chief pillar.

ŚGS 3.2.9: To him [the child] let the young boy, the calf, and the bird go; to him let the flowing liquor go from the jar, and the curds from the vessels. ŚGS 3.3.1: Right here, O pillar, do thou stand firm—stable, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in woolly sheep.

Stand in safety, O you who are sprinkled with ghee; stand right here, you who are well-established, rich in sesame, and possessed of courtyards. May they be satisfied in the midst of prosperity; let not those who seek to harm reach you. Cows are summoned here; goats and sheep are summoned.
"Then, invited with the sweet essence of food, may you be established in our houses;
take your stand in the *Rathantara*, rest in the *Vāmadevya*, and be supported by the *Bṛhat*. With these words, he touches the king of pillars.
He then touches the pillars of the measured structure.
ŚGS 3.3.3: "Truth and faith," [he should place] in the east;
ŚGS 3.3.4: "Sacrifice and sacrificial fee," in the south; ŚGS 3.3.5:
"Strength and vigor," in the west.
ŚGS_3.3.6: On the north [side], he should offer [the oblation] with the words, "The Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.
ŚGS_3.3.7: [He should offer] with the words, "The Stūpa of Fortune, the King who is the Pillar of Dharma.
ŚGS_3.3.8: The two door-panels [he should offer] as Day and Night.
ŚGS 3.3.9: A year is the covering. ŚGS 3.3.10: With the words "The bull, the ocean," he should bury an anointed stone beneath the stūpa. ŚGS 3.4.0: Now follows the rite for entering the house.

In the rite for Vāstoṣpati: having kindled the domestic fire outside with the mantra, "I place the fire with a gracious mind; may it be the gatherer of riches. Do not harm our elder, nor our child; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds," ŚGS_3.4.1: [This is] the rite for Vāstoṣpati. ŚGS_3.4.2: Having kindled the domestic fire outside with the mantra, "I place the fire with a gracious mind; may it be the gatherer of riches. Do not harm our elder, nor our child; be auspicious to our bipeds and auspicious to our quadrupeds," [he performs the following].
ŚGS 3.4.3: Having established a new water-pot upon nine *kuśa* grasses with their tips pointing eastward;
ŚGS 3.4.4: Having consecrated it with the mantra, "May our heroes be unharmed; may our wealth not be poured away"; ŚGS 3.4.5:
In the forenoon, he offers three oblations using the *stotriya* of the *Rathantara*, repeating it and forming the *kakup* meter.
Regarding the recitation of a *pragātha* to form three verses, see *Īṣṭisūtra* viii.25. The *stotriya* for the *rathantara* is *Ṛgveda* vii.32.22ff.;
that for the *vāmadevya* is iv.31.1–3;
and that for the *bṛhat* is vi.46.1ff. (cf. SBEN p.95, n. 5–7).
ŚGS 3.4.6: [The offering] of the Vāmadevya [Sāman] at midday; ŚGS 3.4.7: [The offering] of the Bṛhat [Sāman] in the afternoon; ŚGS 3.4.8:

At night, there is the offering of the cooked oblation (*sthālīpāka*) consisting of ten verses: the four Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), the three beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling" (*vāstoṣpate*), "O Lord of the Dwelling, the remover of disease" (*amīvahā vāstoṣpate*), and "O Lord of the Dwelling, firm pillar" (*vāstoṣpate dhruvā sthūṇā*), and the tenth verse dedicated to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

ŚGS 3.4.9: Taking his eldest son and his wife, he should set out with his grain. ŚGS 3.4.10: "The houses of Indra are auspicious, wealthy, and protective; those I enter together with my wife, together with my offspring, together with my cattle, together with the increase of wealth, and with whatever else I possess. ŚGS 3.5.1: "What is favorable, what is helpful, what is auspicious, what is auspicious—for your security and for peace, I enter. May there be fearlessness for us. May the village deliver me to the forest; O All-Great One, deliver me [from the forest]. Thus he speaks when departing from the village.
ŚGS 3.5.2: "May the forest entrust me to the village; may the great universe entrust me to you," [he says] when entering the village, provided he is not empty-handed.

ŚGS 3.5.3: "I enter auspicious and well-disposed houses, which do not destroy heroes but possess many heroes. Carrying refreshment and sprinkling ghee, may I dwell with a happy mind in these other [houses]. This is always to be recited upon entering.
ŚGS 3.6.0: Now, the sacrifice for one going on a journey.
ŚGS 3.6.1: One who has not established the sacred fires, when about to depart, looks at his house. ŚGS 3.6.2: "O Mitra and Varuṇa, protect these houses of mine!"
"May Pūṣan protect these [grains], unspoiled and undecayed, until our return.
He also mutters, "We have come back upon the path.
Then, having returned from his journey, he looks toward his home.

O houses, do not fear; do not tremble. Bearing strength, we come. Bearing strength, with a benevolent mind and wise intent, I approach your houses, rejoicing in my heart. Those from whom one who is away longs, and in whom there is much goodwill—we call upon those houses. May they recognize us as we recognize them. Cows are summoned here; goats and sheep are summoned.
And the sweet essence of food is summoned into our houses.

Having worshipped the domestic fire with the mantra: "This venerable Agni is ours; he is more venerable than we. By approaching him, may we not suffer harm; may he establish us in excellence," one should utter auspicious speech.
"Thou art the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj; [may] the milking of Virāj be in my feet"—with these words, he receives the water for washing the feet (*pādya*).
Now follows the *Āgrayaṇa* offering.

One who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), when about to eat new grain, should offer it into the domestic fire (*gṛhya-agni*) with the exclamation *svāhā*, dedicated to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth.

making the last verse the final one.

ŚGS 4.1.2: Having seated an odd number of Brāhmaṇas who are knowers of the Vedas—at least three, and not fewer—facing the south as if they were the ancestors.
ŚGS 4.1.3: Having scattered sesame seeds into an odd number of water-vessels.

ŚGS 4.1.10: Some [place the balls] in front.

ŚGS 4.2.1: Now, therefore, the Ekoddiṣṭa.

ŚGS 4.9.0: Now follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

ŚGS 4.9.3: May Agni be satisfied; may Vāyu be satisfied; may Sūrya be satisfied; may Viṣṇu be satisfied; may Prajāpati be satisfied; may Virūpākṣa be satisfied; may Sahasrākṣa be satisfied; may Soma, Brahmā, the Vedas, the gods, the ṛṣis, and all the meters; Om-kāra, Vaṣaṭ-kāra, the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis), the Sāvitrī, the sacrifices, Heaven and Earth, the constellations, the atmosphere, days and nights, the numbers, the twilights, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, the fields, the herbs, the trees, the gandharvas, the apsarases, the nāgas, and all beings ending with these—may they be satisfied. The Śatarcins, the Mādhyamas, Gṛtsamada, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Vāmadeva, Atri, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha, the Pragāthas, the Pavamānas, the Kṣudrasūkta and Mahāsūktas; Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, Paila, the Sūtras, the Bhāṣyas, Gārgya, Babhru, Bābhravya, Maṇḍu, Māṇḍavya, Gārgī Vācaknavī, Vaḍavā Prātitheyī, Sulabhā Maitreyī, Kahola Kauṣītaki, Mahākauṣītaki, Suyajña Śāṅkhāyana, Āśvalāyana, Aitareya, Mahāaitareya, Bhāradvāja, Jātūkarṇya, Paiṅgya, Mahāpaiṅgya, Bāṣkala, Gārgya, and Śākalya.

ŚGS_4.11.2: Not toward the sun at the two junctions of time (dawn and dusk).
ŚGS_4.11.3: Not toward one who is untrustworthy.
ŚGS_4.11.4: Not toward one who performs improper acts.

ŚGS_4.11.7: Nor with these [others].

ŚGS 4.11.11: Not the remainder.

ŚGS 4.11.13: His livelihood may consist of gathering gleanings, receiving gifts without asking, requesting from virtuous people, or officiating at sacrifices.

ŚGS_4.11.17: He should approach his own wife during her season.
ŚGS_4.11.18: He should not sleep during the day. ŚGS_4.11.19: Nor should he sleep during the first or the last part of the night.
ŚGS_4.11.20: He shall not sit on the bare ground. ŚGS_4.11.21: He shall always carry water with him. ŚGS_4.11.22:
He shall wear the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder.
One should not be separated from the teacher,
except by [his] command or with his permission.
Day after day, he should pay homage to his teacher;
and also to his other elders;
and upon meeting a person learned in the Vedas.
ŚGS 4.12.4: Upon returning from a journey, [he should do so] for one who is not a *śrotriya*. ŚGS 4.12.5:

while grasping the other's hands with the words "So-and-so," he invokes a blessing upon him.

ŚGS 4.12.10: He should not point out [faults] by gathering together.

ŚGS 4.12.12: He should not wander alone.
ŚGS 4.12.13: Not naked. ŚGS 4.12.14: Nor with hands covered. ŚGS 4.12.15: One should circumambulate the temples of the gods clockwise.
ŚGS_4.12.16: One should not run. ŚGS_4.12.17: One should not spit. ŚGS_4.12.18: One should not scratch oneself.
ŚGS 4.12.19: One should not look at urine or excrement.
ŚGS 4.12.20: One should sit with one's head covered.
ŚGS 4.12.21: Not on ground that is not covered.
ŚGS 4.12.22: If he has only one garment, he should place the sacrificial thread over his ear.
ŚGS 4.12.23: He should not face the sun. ŚGS 4.12.24: Nor should he face behind it.
During the day he should face north, and at night he should face south.
He should not discharge phlegm into water, nor near it.
He should not climb a tree.
One should not look down into a well;
one should not go to a forest grove; and one should certainly not go to a cremation ground.
ŚGS_4.12.31: He should bathe every day while wearing his clothes. ŚGS_4.12.32: Having bathed, he should put on another garment without having first dried himself.
ŚGS_4.13.0: Now follows the work of agriculture.
ŚGS 4.13.1: Under the asterism Rohiṇī, one should have agricultural work performed.

ŚGS 4.14.0: Now follows the ritual for the boat.

ŚGS 4.14.2: He offers three handfuls of water into the waters, saying: "Homage to the Ocean, the son of Vena; homage to Varuṇa, the lord of dharma; homage, homage to all rivers! ŚGS 4.14.3: Having murmured, "May Viśvakarman, the father of them all, accept the offered oblation," he concludes.
ŚGS 4.14.4: [Water] should be drawn from flowing rivers against the current, and from still waters upwards.

ŚGS 4.15.0: Now follows the rite of the *Śravaṇā* [full moon].

ŚGS 4.15.2: "To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Śravaṇā, svāhā! To the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, svāhā! To the rains, svāhā! ŚGS 4.15.3:
Having kindled the domestic fire outside [the house] and having mixed fried grains (*lāja*) and parched barley flour with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*), he makes the offering.
"To the lord of the divine serpents, svāhā! To the divine serpents, svāhā! (ŚGS 4.15.4).
Having placed a new water-pot on fresh kuśa grass with its tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire (ŚGS 4.15.5), he pours out water, saying:

"May the lord of the divine serpents cover [the child]; may the divine serpents cover [him]," with these words he offers a thread of wool.
"May the lord of the divine serpents anoint [him]; may the divine serpents anoint [him]," with these words he applies collyrium by means of a young *kuśa* blade.
"May the lord of the divine serpents look [at him]; may the divine serpents look [at him]," with these words he causes him to gaze at a mirror.

ŚGS 5.1.0: Now, the mounting [of the fires].

ŚGS 5.1.2: With the mantra "Come, ascend into my vital breaths," he does so once each time; twice silently. ŚGS 5.1.3: Or he heats the two fire-drills with the mantra "This is your womb. ŚGS 5.1.4: Or he heats a fuel-stick.

ŚGS 5.1.8: When the fire has gone out, having offered all the expiatory oblations (*sarva-prāyaścitta-āhuti*), [he offers with the mantras]: "Protect us, O Agni, for our growth, svāhā! ŚGS 5.2.0: Now follows the ritual of dismissal (*utsarga*).
ŚGS 5.2.1: Now, regarding lotus ponds, wells, and tanks;

ŚGS_5.5.5: And upon other portents.
Having cooked a sacrificial oblation of rice (caru) with milk,
[he should do so] in the milk of a cow that has a calf of the same color; however, he must not use the milk of a black cow.
ŚGS 5.5.9: He should offer oblations with each verse of the *Rātrisūkta*.

ŚGS 5.5.10: Having consumed the remnants of the oblation with the *Mahāvyāhṛtis*, ŚGS 5.5.11: [He should touch] his two ears with the mantra, "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ... (May we hear what is auspicious with our ears...).
ŚGS 5.5.12: Having consecrated himself with the mantra, "A hundred autumns are before us, O gods," ŚGS 5.5.13:
he should give something to the Brāhmaṇas.
ŚGS 5.6.1: When a disease has arisen.
ŚGS 5.6.2: With the verse, "These [oblations] for the powerful Rudra, the one with matted hair," he should offer a sacrificial pap made of *gavedhuka* grass, reciting it verse by verse.
ŚGS 5.7.1: If she should give birth before the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) has been performed;

having offered oblations with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, the fire-offering is performed as before. ŚGS 5.8.1:

"—for them let there be a world, *svadhā*, obeisance, and may the sacrifice be prepared among the gods! Those who are equal and of one mind, my living ones among the living..."

ŚGS 5.11.2: Then, having fasted for three nights, one should perform the Mahāśānti rite; one should perform the Mahāśānti rite.
ŚGS 6.1.0: Rules for Private Vedic Study and the Āraṇyaka.

ŚGS 6.1.1: Now, therefore, having paid homage to Brahmā, the Brahman-sage, the source of the Veda; to Indra, Prajāpati, Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Kahola, Kauṣītaki, Mahākauṣītaki, Suyajña, Śāṅkhāyana, Āśvalāyana, Aitareya, Mahāaitareya, Kātyāyana, Śāṭyāyana, Śākalya, Babhru, Bābhravya, Maṇḍu, Māṇḍavya, and indeed to all the former teachers, we shall set forth the rules for private study (*svādhyāya*) and the *Āraṇyaka*.
ŚGS 6.1.2: Having undertaken celibacy for a day and night, the teacher shall abstain from meat.
ŚGS 6.1.3: Raw flesh, a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, and the sight of blood or a hand severed at the wrist are occasions for the suspension of Vedic study.
ŚGS 6.1.4: And likewise when there are corpses or their likenesses.
ŚGS 6.1.5: [One should not recite] those [mantras] which would enter the mouth. ŚGS 6.1.6: [One should not recite] after having vomited or after performing the rite of shaving the beard.
ŚGS 6.1.7: [One should not recite] during the eating of meat, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, or when eating food from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*).
ŚGS 6.1.8: Days that are not separated by village study [are considered a single period].
ŚGS 6.1.9: A period of three nights when no [study] is scheduled.
ŚGS 6.1.10: When touched by another [person].
ŚGS 6.1.11: Also during the days following the intermediate parvans.
ŚGS 6.1.12: And when fire, lightning, thunder, rain, or the appearance of great clouds occurs.
ŚGS 6.1.13: And when there is a wind that carries pebbles, for as long as it lasts.
ŚGS 6.2.1: One should not study for the four months following the full moon of Āṣāḍha.
ŚGS 6.2.2: These are the restrictive rules, including the absolute prohibition regarding the Śakvarī verses.
ŚGS 6.2.3: Having approached an auspicious place in the north-eastern direction (aparājitā), prior to the appearance of the morning light.
ŚGS 6.2.4: Fetching water before sunrise. ŚGS 6.2.5: And entering the ritual circle with this *ṛc* verse: "O you who possess the fragrance of ointment.
ŚGS 6.2.6: The ritual circle, however, should have its entrance to the east or to the north; it should be free from the presence of women, of no fixed measure, and spacious.
ŚGS 6.2.7: [The recitation of] the Āvāmadevya hymn and the subsequent pacification (śānti).
ŚGS 6.2.8: And the request for instruction once again.
ŚGS 6.2.9: Having sipped water (ācamana) while standing outside the ritual circle (maṇḍala).
ŚGS 6.2.10: They should recite [the verses] after having performed the rites of pacification (śānti).
ŚGS 6.2.11: If the vessel for the pacification rite is damaged, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is the expiation.
ŚGS 6.2.12: The sprinkling, however, is to be done with a hand holding gold or holding a bunch of *darbha* grass.
Thus ends the section on recitation.
Now, having entered the maṇḍala,
the teacher sits facing east, while the others sit to his south facing north, according to their rank.
ŚGS_6.3.3: In the absence [of such persons], those facing all directions [should wait].
ŚGS_6.3.4: They should await the rising of the sun. ŚGS_6.3.5: And having recognized that it possesses rays of light, [they should proceed].

ŚGS 6.3.6: [The student] should grasp the feet of the teacher—having been washed—with his right hands holding the teacher’s right foot and his left hands holding the left, while his right hands are placed above.
ŚGS 6.3.7: Then, having placed [the water] into the vessel of peace (*śāntipātra*) containing stalks of *dūrvā* grass, they should begin their recitation with hands that do not splash the water.
ŚGS 6.3.8: This is the rule; however, if they should become weary, one of them should keep the vessel of peace from being empty.
ŚGS_6.3.9: And at the beginning and end of each chapter, all [the verses] are recited.
ŚGS_6.3.10: That [recitation] becomes continuous and uninterrupted.
ŚGS_6.3.11: Now follows the rite for pacification (śānti).
ŚGS 6.3.12: The syllable *om*, the great utterances (*mahā-vyāhṛti*), the Sāvitrī, the Rathantara, the Bṛhat, the Vāmadevya, the Punarādāya, and the Kakup-form—these are the Bṛhat and Rathantara.
ŚGS 6.3.13: These ten become completed.
ŚGS 6.3.14: "The Virāj consists of tens"—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage.

ŚGS 6.4.1: "Unerring, swift-minded, and keen-eyed; Sūrya, the best of lights—O Consecration, do not harm me! With these words, they gaze at the sun. ŚGS 6.4.2: "The two of you [drank] the surā" is one verse, and "May there be well-being for us on our paths," etc., are three verses; these belong to the Mahāvrata rite. ŚGS 6.4.3: However, those of the Śakvarī meters come first.

ŚGS_6.4.4: "To him who desires to drink," "O you who are wealthy, the wealthiest," and "That one of yours which is not to be slain"—these are three triplets; and "To this very one, of this soma-juice" and "For thus indeed you are a seeker of heroes"—these are on both sides of the *śakvarī* verses.
ŚGS_6.4.5: Now, regarding the *upaniṣads*.
ŚGS_6.4.6: Those [verses] belonging to the *mahāvrata* in this manner.

ŚGS 6.4.7: For those who have received the *saṃhitā*, however, the distinction is that they shall first say, "I will speak the Ṛta; I will speak the Truth. ŚGS 6.4.8: Then, for the *mantha* [mixture], [they recite] "We choose that of Savitṛ" (*tat savitur vṛṇīmahe*) and "That desirable [splendor] of Savitṛ" (*tat savitur vareṇyam*), as well as the preceding verses. ŚGS 6.4.9: Then follow the peace-chants (*śānti*) pertaining to the office, beginning with "The unassailable mind" (*adabdhaṃ manaḥ*).
Thus ends the daily observance (āhnika). Now, at the time of rising, having cast off evil and performed the constant rite of pacification (śānti), [one should proceed].
ŚGS 6.4.13: They look at the sun, reciting: "The risen one has bestowed the *śukriya*. ŚGS 6.5.1: [They look] at themselves, reciting three times: "Him (the sun) I place within myself.
ŚGS 6.5.2: "May prosperity attend me; may glory attend me. May prosperity follow me; may glory follow me."
ŚGS 6.5.3: "Accompanied by Indra, with his retinue, with his strength, with his glory, and with his vigor, may I rise up from this seat," saying thus, he rises.
ŚGS 6.5.4: Having risen, [he says], "May prosperity rise for me; may glory rise for me. ŚGS 6.5.5:
Shaking out the hem of his garment, [he says], "I shake off this hateful rival, evil, and misfortune."

[They recite] the hymn *apa prācaḥ*; the two verses beginning with *indraś ca mṛḷayāti naḥ*; the one verse beginning with *yata indra bhayāmahe*; and the verse *śāsa itthā mahān asi* facing east; *svastidā* facing south, turning to the right; *virakṣaḥ* facing west; and *vi na indra* facing north, turning to the left; and *apa indra* facing south, turning to the right. They gaze upward toward the sky.
Having worshipped the Sun with the verse *savitā paścātāt*, they worship the Sun with the verse *tac cakṣuḥ*.
Turning back, they return and sit down.
Taking water from the vessel of peace (*śāntipātra*) with the words, "The waters are peaceful," they pour it onto the ground.
ŚGS 6.6.5: With the words, "As the earth," they draw [the ashes] toward themselves.
ŚGS 6.6.6: With the words, "Thus may peace be in me," he smears [the ashes] on his right shoulder.
ŚGS 6.6.7: He does so a second time.
ŚGS 6.6.8: In this manner, the third [verse].

ŚGS 6.6.9: "From joint to joint you arise; from joint to joint you grow. Be auspicious to us, O *śālī* (rice plant). Having taken a stalk of *dūrvā* grass and placed it upon his head [with these words], ŚGS 6.6.10:

"May Agni be satisfied; may Vāyu be satisfied; may Sūrya be satisfied; may Viṣṇu be satisfied; may Prajāpati be satisfied; may Virūpākṣa be satisfied; may Sahasrākṣa be satisfied; may all beings be satisfied. Thus [he says].
ŚGS 6.6.11: [He pays homage to] the teachers beginning with Sumantu, Jaimini, Vaiśampāyana, and Paila.
ŚGS 6.6.12: [He pays homage to] his own ancestors.
ŚGS 6.6.13: Having thus poured out water, [he continues].
Having recited the Vāmadevya hymn,
they disperse according to their desire.

May there be for us fearlessness, peace, and well-being, proceeding from the power of tradition, wisdom, revelation, and memory, established without dispute and free from fear. Homage be to the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans! May they increase our auspiciousness, long life, physical form, health, tranquility, freedom from misfortune, imperishability, vigor, splendor, fame, strength, Vedic luster, renown, longevity, progeny, and cattle. May those who offer homage cause these to increase; may they protect me from ill-praised or ill-employed [mantras], and from all that is deficient or redundant. May the gods and sages protect me; may Brahman and Truth protect me—may Brahman and Truth protect me.
